question: Can a small set of human similarity judgments improve the global organization and transfer utility of pretrained visual representations without destroying their useful local geometry?

key_findings.claim: Naively maximizing human alignment harms transfer because it restructures local neighborhoods too aggressively.
key_findings.evidence: A square linear transform is trained on 4.70 million THINGS odd-one-out judgments over 1,854 objects. The alignment-only transform substantially raises held-out human agreement but average five-shot performance falls—for CLIP ViT-L/14 WIT, from 67.71% to 47.62%.

key_findings.claim: gLocal jointly preserves original neighborhood probabilities and aligns global human similarity structure.
key_findings.evidence: Its objective combines triplet negative log likelihood, a contrastive local loss between original and transformed similarity distributions, and shrinkage toward a scaled identity. Hyperparameters are selected by alignment cross-validation.

key_findings.claim: The transform improves few-shot and nearest-neighbor anomaly detection for image-text models across many datasets.
key_findings.evidence: For CLIP ViT-L/14 WIT, average five-shot accuracy rises 67.71% to 69.91% and anomaly AUROC 90.16% to 95.19%. Individual coarse/subpopulation tasks often improve markedly, though fine-grained datasets and ImageNet-supervised representations are inconsistent.

key_findings.claim: Human alignment transfers across four judgment datasets with little loss versus naive alignment, but the supervision reflects limited populations, images and concepts.
key_findings.evidence: gLocal nearly matches the naive transform on THINGS held-out accuracy and RSA correlations for King, Cichy and Peterson datasets. Human-adversarial triplets fail to reproduce gains, supporting a human-structure interpretation, while the paper acknowledges annotation cost and incomplete conceptual coverage.

method.core_idea: Apply a post-hoc linear map that inserts human global semantic organization while distilling each model's original local similarity distribution.
method.mechanism: Fit triplet likelihood on human odd-one-out data, regularize the matrix toward scaled identity, match softmax neighborhood distributions over ImageNet through a contrastive local loss, then freeze the transform for downstream few-shot and k-NN anomaly tasks.
assumptions: Crowd odd-one-out judgments encode transferable global visual-semantic structure.
The source representation already contains the concepts needed for linear reorganization.
Preserving soft local neighborhoods retains downstream-relevant information.
The cross-validated human-alignment objective selects a useful global/local tradeoff.

techniques.role: Fits global similarity from odd-one-out behavior.
Preserves the source embedding's local probability geometry.
Reuses frozen representations without retraining the encoder.

evaluations.setting: CLIP RN50/ViT models trained on WIT or LAION, plus ImageNet models, across six five-shot tasks.
evaluations.metric: Classification accuracy averaged over five runs.
evaluations.result: gLocal generally improves image-text models, especially coarse tasks, while naive alignment strongly harms accuracy; ImageNet encoders gain inconsistently.
evaluations.baseline: Original, naive/global alignment and Tip-Adapter combinations.

evaluations.setting: Standard and distribution-shift semantic anomaly detection.
evaluations.result: gLocal improves nearly every image-text model/dataset pair and reaches or approaches selected SOTA results without task-specific outlier data.
evaluations.baseline: Original representations, naive transform and external methods that may use outlier exposure or textual supervision.

evaluations.metric: Held-out odd-one-out accuracy and representational-similarity Spearman correlation.
evaluations.result: gLocal retains nearly all the alignment of the naive transform while preserving downstream performance.

limitations: Human judgments are costly and cover only 1,854 natural-object images.
Crowd similarity reflects cultural, demographic and task framing choices and is not universal ground truth.
Benefits are inconsistent for ImageNet-supervised encoders and some fine-grained tasks.
The square transform can be large and model-specific, requiring separate fitting per representation.
Hyperparameters are selected for alignment rather than downstream generalization, and many tasks/datasets are tested.
Nearest-neighbor anomaly benchmarks do not establish robustness or safety in deployed open-set settings.
Post-hoc linear alignment does not prove that human-like global structure caused human generalization.
failure_modes: The source model lacks a human concept, so no linear transform can recover it.
Preserving original neighborhoods retains harmful shortcuts or biases.
Human global similarity collapses distinctions necessary for fine-grained recognition.
A biased judgment panel imposes culturally narrow concepts and worsens other users' tasks.
Alignment gains overfit the finite image set despite object-disjoint evaluation.
reusable_insights: Global representation alignment should be constrained by local-geometry preservation.
Report human agreement and downstream utility separately; optimizing one can damage the other.
Use adversarial or shuffled human judgments to test whether gains come from meaningful structure rather than regularization alone.
Evaluate alignment across populations, domains and tasks before calling it human-like.
open_questions: Can diverse or personalized similarity panels produce controllable representation geometries?
Can global/local alignment be incorporated during pretraining without retaining source shortcuts?
What is the minimum judgment budget and how should triplets be actively selected?
Do gains transfer to detection, segmentation, embodied perception and nonvisual modalities?

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating (and Improving) the Correspondence Between Deep Neural Networks and Human Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Peterson et al. fit feature transformations to human similarities and study cognitive prediction; gLocal explicitly protects local embedding structure and evaluates practical few-shot/anomaly transfer.

competitive_landscape.title: Transforming Neural Network Visual Representations to Predict Human Judgments of Similarity
competitive_landscape.difference: Attarian et al. improve prediction of human choices with expressive and asymmetric transforms; the reviewed method targets global alignment that preserves machine neighborhoods and downstream utility.

competitive_landscape.title: Human alignment of neural network representations
competitive_landscape.difference: The predecessor maps which training choices affect human alignment and shows cross-dataset linear transfer; gLocal adds the locality constraint and demonstrates downstream performance gains.

competitive_landscape.title: Alignment with human representations supports robust few-shot learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This work predicts and observes a U-shaped alignment/performance relation across 491 existing models; gLocal performs a causal-looking post-hoc intervention but on a smaller set of encoders and tasks.

novelty_assessment: The local-geometry preservation term is a simple but important advance over prior human-alignment transforms, and the downstream results show that human judgments can act as useful global supervision. The causal and universality claims should remain modest: benefits depend on source representations and tasks, and one finite behavioral dataset cannot define humanity's visual organization.
reviewer_notes: Read all 30 pages, including objectives, hyperparameter selection, per-task tables, adversarial-human ablation, ImageNet failures, compute and RSA appendices. Four primary direct predecessors/comparators were checked on 2026-08-23.
